content: Excessive alcohol consumption during pregnancy is linked to harmful effects on both the mother and the baby. It is crucial to create and assess effective interventions during this critical period in a woman's life. However, to date, no systematic reviews of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have been conducted in this specific population. The objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness of psychosocial interventions for pregnant women enrolled in alcohol treatment programs. The focus was on improving birth and neonatal outcomes, promoting maternal abstinence from alcohol, and enhancing retention in treatment programs. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Drugs and Alcohol Group's Trial Register (up to December 2007), MEDLINE (1950–2007), PsycINFO (1806–2007), EMBASE (1974–2007), and CINAHL (1982–2007). The inclusion criteria required randomized or quasi-randomized studies that compared psychosocial interventions with pharmacological treatments, placebo, no intervention, or other psychosocial interventions for treating alcohol dependence during pregnancy. Three independent reviewers assessed the identified studies for inclusion using standardized data extraction and quality assessment tools. The search yielded 958 citations, of which 17 were considered relevant for full-text review. An additional 9 articles were identified through manual reference searches, resulting in a total of 26 articles for evaluation. However, after thorough review, none of the articles met the inclusion criteria for the study. Consequently, data extraction and quality assessment could not be performed. The authors concluded that the research question remains unanswered due to the absence of relevant randomized controlled trials. There is a significant need for high-quality RCTs to evaluate the effectiveness of psychosocial interventions for pregnant women undergoing alcohol treatment.
